solutionSource.check: grid rebuilt from the blog's light list (unique); every answer written into it with each crossing agreeing

entries.clue: Building propositions (8)

blocks.note: the noun: a business's building and grounds
the logician's sense: statements an argument starts from

annotation.walkthrough: Two words side by side with nothing joining them: 'Building' is the noun, not the activity.
annotation.definitionFit: Premises covers both the property a business occupies and the statements a conclusion rests on, two unrelated senses of one word.

entries.clue: Dishes requiring significant time in cookware (7)

indicatorNotes.in: 'in' says one thing sits inside another, as the time sits inside the cookware

blocks.note: an age is a long stretch of time

annotation.surface: A recipe warning that these dishes need a long spell in the pans.
annotation.walkthrough: The surface is a cooking instruction, and the wordplay does literally what it says: the time goes into the pots.
annotation.definitionFit: Potage is the French word for a thick soup, taken into English; soups are dishes, so this is a definition by example.

entries.clue: Bringing forth end of lucrative career (9)

indicatorNotes.end of: the end of a word is its final letter, here the E of 'lucrative'

blocks.note: a vocation is a calling or career

annotation.surface: Talk of bringing a well-paid career to a close.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Bringing forth end of' reads as a single phrase about ending something; the definition stops after 'forth'.
annotation.definitionFit: To evoke is to call forth, so evocation is the bringing forth of a memory or feeling: a plain synonym, noun for noun.

entries.clue: Fashionable drink, regularly kinda bland (7)

indicatorNotes.regularly: at regular intervals, so every other letter of 'kinda'

blocks.note: a sip is a small drink

annotation.surface: A verdict on a trendy cocktail that turns out kind of dull.
annotation.walkthrough: The surface is a fair review in itself: a fashionable drink that tastes of nothing.
annotation.definitionFit: A plain synonym: both words describe food, or company, with no flavour or interest.

entries.clue: Possible material (7)

blocks.note: only in negatives: 'no ___ reason' means no possible reason
of this world, material rather than spiritual

annotation.walkthrough: The first sense only lives in negatives: 'no earthly use' means no possible use.
annotation.definitionFit: An idiomatic sense (no earthly chance) and a plain one (earthly goods, worldly and material) of the same word.

entries.clue: Many, many clubs start to expand immediately (2,4)

indicatorNotes.start to: the start of a word is its first letter, here the E of 'expand'

annotation.surface: A report that a great many clubs are opening branches right now.
annotation.walkthrough: The doubled 'many' is one piece, A TON, not two separate numbers.
annotation.definitionFit: A plain synonym: an adverbial phrase meaning without delay.

entries.clue: Mass of trouble, mostly close to the boarding site (9)

indicatorNotes.mostly: most of a word, so all but its last letter
indicatorNotes.close to: the close of a word is its last letter, here the E of 'the'

blocks.note: AGGRO (British slang for trouble, aggression) without its O
at an airport you board at the gate

annotation.surface: A heap of trouble brewing near the departure gate.
annotation.walkthrough: Aggro is British slang for aggressive trouble-making. 'Boarding site' suggests a building yard; it is the airport gate.
annotation.definitionFit: A plain synonym: an aggregate is a whole formed by massing many units together.

entries.clue: Boring part in exam is elliptic (7)

indicatorNotes.in: 'in' places the boring part inside the exam, word for word

blocks.note: a drill bit is the part that bores
an oral is a spoken exam

annotation.surface: A student complaining that part of the exam is dull and obscure.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Boring' pretends to be a complaint about the exam; it is the drilling kind of boring.
annotation.definitionFit: Planetary orbits are ellipses, so the setter uses elliptic loosely for 'to do with orbits'.

entries.clue: Large crater about to envelop tree (7)

indicatorNotes.to envelop: to envelop is to wrap round, so the 'about' letters go around the tree

annotation.surface: A huge crater on the point of swallowing a tree.
annotation.walkthrough: 'About' is the Latin circa, abbreviated ca. as in dates, not a sign of reversal.
annotation.definitionFit: A caldera is the wide basin left when a volcano collapses; 'large crater' is the dictionary gloss.

entries.clue: Misappropriating time to stir up criminal group (10)

blocks.note: to rouse is to stir up

annotation.surface: A crime story about stealing while agitating a gang.
annotation.walkthrough: Trousering is British slang for pocketing money, especially dishonestly.
annotation.definitionFit: A British informal sense: to trouser cash is to put it in your trouser pocket, usually improperly.

entries.clue: Bad temper is, on reflection, somewhat deliberate (4)

indicatorNotes.on reflection: a reflection shows things backwards, as in a mirror
indicatorNotes.somewhat: somewhat means to some extent, so only part of 'deliberate'

annotation.surface: A remark that someone's bad temper is, if you think about it, rather calculated.
annotation.walkthrough: 'On reflection' sounds like thinking again; it means read backwards.
annotation.definitionFit: Bile was the humour thought to cause irritability, so the word stands for bad temper by old medical association.

entries.clue: At length, Peter’s struggling to tackle an unpleasant task (5,3,6)

indicatorNotes.struggling: struggling letters thrash about out of order, so rearrange them

annotation.surface: Peter labouring for a long time over a chore he dreads.
annotation.walkthrough: 'At length' looks like a time phrase; every letter of it is fodder.
annotation.definitionFit: An idiom: a nettle stings less if seized firmly, so grasping it means facing a difficulty boldly.

entries.clue: Disproportionately long drive duly taking hours in the middle (7)

indicatorNotes.taking: taking something away from a word removes letters from it
indicatorNotes.in the middle: the centre of 'hours' is its third letter, U

blocks.note: a spin is a drive in a car

blocks.clueFragment: duly taking hours in the middle
blocks.note: DULY with U, the middle of hoUrs, taken out

annotation.surface: A long drive that duly takes hours.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Taking' looks like 'lasting'; here it means removing, and what goes is the middle letter of 'hours', not the hours.
annotation.definitionFit: Spindly describes limbs or stems long and thin out of proportion, so the two-word gloss is fair.

entries.clue: The most solitary single person remains overwhelmed by extremes of lust (9)

indicatorNotes.overwhelmed by: to be overwhelmed is to be engulfed, so the outer letters close over ONE LIES
indicatorNotes.extremes of: the extremes of a word are its first and last letters

annotation.surface: A lonely soul left overcome by desire.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Remains' is a verb here, not the noun for what is left over.
annotation.definitionFit: A plain synonym in the superlative: lonely and solitary both mean alone.

entries.clue: Everything far to the right of hotel entrance area (7)

indicatorNotes.to the right of: in an across entry, right means after, so ALL WAY follows H

blocks.note: H = hotel in the phonetic alphabet

annotation.surface: Directions to a spot well to the right of the hotel.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Far to the right' looks like one phrase; 'far' is WAY and 'to the right of' places the pieces after hotel.
annotation.definitionFit: A plain description: the hallway is the space just inside a front door.

entries.clue: Enormous barrier managing to eliminate cold (9)

indicatorNotes.to eliminate: to eliminate is to get rid of, so C comes out of COPING

annotation.surface: A huge wall being built to keep out the cold.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Managing to' reads as 'succeeding in'; 'managing' is COPING and 'to eliminate' acts on it.
annotation.definitionFit: An informal synonym: a walloping great thing is a whopping, enormous one.

entries.clue: Does medical department provide authorisation? (7)

blocks.note: to do someone is to con them
ENT = ear, nose and throat department

annotation.surface: A patient asking whether the hospital department grants permission.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Does' opens the clue as a question word; it is the verb meaning swindles.
annotation.definitionFit: A plain synonym, apt to the hospital surface, where a patient's consent authorises treatment.

entries.clue: Misdemeanour relating to part of course (7)

blocks.note: a fence is an obstacle on a racecourse

annotation.surface: A minor offence connected with a stretch of a course.
annotation.walkthrough: The course is a racecourse with jumps, not a course of study.
annotation.definitionFit: A misdemeanour is a minor crime, a particular kind of breach of the law.

entries.clue: What may be the focus of speech therapy to begin with, say? (7)

annotation.definition: What may be the focus of speech therapy to begin with, say?

indicatorNotes.to begin with: the beginnings of words are their first letters

blocks.note: the first letters of Speech Therapy

annotation.surface: A question about what speech therapy tends to address.
annotation.walkthrough: The whole clue defines the answer while its words also build it; the question mark flags that a stutter is only one possible focus.
annotation.definitionFit: Read straight, the clue asks what a speech therapist might work on first, and a stammer is the classic case.

entries.clue: Black birds and dogs (7)

annotation.surface: A list of dark birds and some dogs.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Black birds' looks like blackbirds; black is only its abbreviation.
annotation.definitionFit: A definition by example: the beagle is one breed of hound.

entries.clue: One can be charged for assault (7)

blocks.note: charged with electricity, not with a crime
the legal term for unlawful physical attack

annotation.surface: A legal point that someone can face a charge of assault.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Charged' reads as the courtroom sense because of 'assault'; the first definition means charged with electricity.
annotation.definitionFit: An electrical cell stores charge, and in law assault and battery go together as the crimes of threat and blow.

entries.clue: A rugby player (huge, incidentally) (7)

blocks.note: a prop is a front-row forward in rugby

annotation.surface: A remark in passing that a rugby player is huge.
annotation.walkthrough: The brackets make 'incidentally' look like an aside; it is the definition.
annotation.definitionFit: Used alone to change the subject, apropos works as 'by the way', which is what incidentally means.

entries.clue: Maximally upsetting news ultimately set dad off (7)

indicatorNotes.ultimately: ultimately means in the end, so the last letter of 'news'
indicatorNotes.off: off as in gone wrong, so the letters are out of order

annotation.surface: The most distressing news finally set Dad off.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Upsetting' sits beside 'news' as if describing it; it belongs to the definition.
annotation.definitionFit: Maximally is the setter's way of asking for a superlative, and sad things are upsetting ones.

entries.clue: What, for example, is a thing kids shouldn’t hear? (4-6,4)

blocks.note: taken literally: count the letters of 'What'

annotation.surface: A parent asking which words children ought not to hear.
annotation.walkthrough: 'What' is not a question word here but the example itself: a word of four letters.
annotation.definitionFit: Literally, 'what' has four letters; idiomatically, the phrase means a swear word, since many are that short.

entries.clue: Difficult problem really hit back (4)

indicatorNotes.back: back means backwards, so the letters run in reverse

blocks.note: to tonk is British slang for hitting hard

annotation.surface: Someone who really struck back at a tough problem.
annotation.walkthrough: Tonk is British slang, often cricket, for a big hit.
annotation.definitionFit: A figurative sense: a knot is a tangle, so a knotty problem is a hard one to undo.

entries.clue: Endeavour to go in with force (10)

blocks.note: to enter is to go in
to prise is to force open

annotation.surface: Trying to break in by force.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Endeavour' looks like a verb before 'to go in'; it is the noun.
annotation.definitionFit: A plain synonym, noun for noun: a bold undertaking. Both are also names of famous ships.

entries.clue: Picked up books by famous limerick writer (6)

indicatorNotes.by: by means beside, so the books stand next to the writer

blocks.note: NT = New Testament, a set of books

annotation.surface: Someone who got hold of books by a famous limerick writer.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Picked up' reads as collecting the books; it means acquiring a skill or fact.
annotation.definitionFit: An informal synonym: you pick up a language or a trick when you learn it without formal study.

entries.clue: Faculty rather restricted by number often rowing? (8)

indicatorNotes.restricted by: to be restricted by something is to be hemmed in by it, so YES sits inside EIGHT

blocks.note: a racing crew is often an eight

annotation.surface: A question about a faculty member whose rowing is limited by a number.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Faculty' hints at a university staff; it is one of the senses.
annotation.definitionFit: A definition by example: sight is one of the faculties, the powers of the body and mind.
